Cheese and Poblano Pepper Strip Tamales

Served at: Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe

Makes 20-24 tamalesPrep 1 hour 30 minCook 1 hour 15 min

Tamales are a beloved and ancient Mesoamerican dish, deeply rooted in Mexican culture and often prepared for special occasions and holidays. For the Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe on December 12th, families gather to honor the Virgin Mary with prayer, celebration, and a feast that frequently includes a variety of tamales, symbolizing community and tradition. These savory cheese and poblano tamales offer a comforting and flavorful addition to the festive table.

Ingredients

  • 40-50 dried corn husks
  • 4-5 large poblano peppers
  • 12 ounces (340g) Oaxaca cheese or Monterey Jack, cut into 1/2-inch (1.25 cm) strips
  • 1 cup (226g) vegetable shortening or lard, at room temperature
  • 4 cups (480g) masa harina for tamales (not regular masa harina for tortillas)
  • 2 teaspoons (10g) baking powder
  • 2 teaspoons (10g) fine sea salt, plus more to taste
  • 3 1/2 to 4 cups (840-960ml) warm chicken or vegetable broth

Method

  1. Soak the corn husks: Place dried corn husks in a large bowl or pot, cover completely with hot water, and weigh down with a plate to keep them submerged. Let them soak for at least 1 hour, or until pliable.
  2. Prepare the poblano peppers: Roast the poblano peppers directly over an open flame (gas burner) or under a broiler until the skin is charred and blistered on all sides. Place the roasted peppers in a bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let steam for 10-15 minutes.
  3. Peel and slice peppers: Once cooled, peel the skin from the peppers, remove the stems and seeds, and slice them into 1/4-inch (6mm) wide strips. Set aside.
  4. Prepare the masa dough: In a large bowl, beat the shortening or lard with an electric mixer on medium-high speed until light and fluffy, about 3-5 minutes.
  5. Combine dry ingredients: In a separate bowl, whisk together the masa harina, baking powder, and salt.
  6. Add masa to shortening: Gradually add the masa harina mixture to the beaten shortening, alternating with the warm broth, mixing until a soft, spreadable dough forms. The dough should be light and fluffy.
  7. Test the masa: To test if the masa is ready, drop a small piece (about 1/2 teaspoon) into a glass of cold water; if it floats, it's ready. If not, beat for another minute or two and retest.
  8. Assemble the tamales: Take a softened corn husk, wider end at the top. Spread about 2-3 tablespoons of masa dough evenly over the wider part of the husk, leaving about 1 inch (2.5 cm) clear at the top and sides.
  9. Add filling: Place a few strips of poblano pepper and 1-2 strips of cheese in the center of the masa.
  10. Fold the tamale: Fold one side of the husk over the filling, then the other side, overlapping slightly. Fold the narrow bottom end of the husk up towards the center. Leave the top open.
  11. Repeat and arrange: Continue assembling tamales until all masa and filling are used.
  12. Prepare for steaming: Arrange the tamales upright in a large steamer basket, open-end facing up. Do not pack them too tightly, as they need room to expand.
  13. Steam the tamales: Place the steamer basket over a pot of simmering water, ensuring the water does not touch the tamales. Cover tightly and steam for 1 hour 15 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes, or until the masa pulls away easily from the husk. Check water level periodically and add more hot water if needed.
  14. Rest and serve: Let the tamales rest for 10-15 minutes off the heat before serving. Serve warm with your favorite salsa.

Tips

  • For extra flavor, use the broth from cooking chicken or vegetables.
  • Ensure your masa dough is light and fluffy; this is key to tender tamales.
  • Don't overcrowd your steamer; steam in batches if necessary for even cooking.
